Good — only the intended files changed (the `data/*.db` files are gitignored). Both `bun run typecheck` and `bun test` pass.

## Summary

The bug was in `app/Http/Controllers/PostController.ts`'s `update` action: it built a raw `Response` with a hardcoded `status: 302` redirect instead of using the controller's `this.redirect()` helper. Per fetch/browser semantics, a 302 response to a non-GET request (the edit form submits a `PUT`) tells the client to replay the *same method* against the `Location` header — so the browser kept re-issuing `PUT /posts/<id>`, hit `posts.update` again, got another 302, and looped until `net::ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS` (the save itself succeeded on the first request, which is why a manual reload showed the new content). `store()` and `destroy()` already used `this.redirect()`, which auto-selects **303** for non-GET requests — 303 always switches the follow-up to `GET`, which is what publishing/deleting already relied on. I changed `update()` to `return this.redirect(\`/posts/${post.id}\`)`, matching the existing pattern, and added a regression test in `tests/PostController.test.ts` that creates a user/post via the ORM, authenticates with `actingAs`/`withCsrf`, `PUT`s an edit, and asserts a 303 redirect to `/posts/<id>`.
